--- title: "Visualizing 2D quantitative data and linear regression" subtitle: "
36-315: Statistical Graphics and Visualization, Summer 2026" footer: "[36-315-summer26.netlify.app](https://36-315-summer26.netlify.app)" format: revealjs: embed-resources: true height: 900 width: 1600 theme: theme.scss smaller: true slide-number: c/t linestretch: 1.4 code-line-numbers: false html-math-method: method: mathjax url: "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3/es5/tex-mml-chtml.js" --- ## Summarizing 2D quantitative data Three aspects: * Direction/trend (positive, negative) * Strength of the relationship (strong, moderate, weak) * Linearity (linear, non-linear) . . . Goals: * describe the relationships between two variables $X$ and $Y$ * describe the conditional distribution $Y \mid X$ via regression analysis * describe the joint distribution $X, Y$ via contours, heatmaps, etc. . . . Big picture ideas: * Scatterplots are by far the most common visual * Regression analysis is by far the most popular analysis * Relationships may vary across other variables, e.g., categorical variables ## Summarizing 2D quantitative data * Numerical summary: correlation coefficient ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} cor(penguins$bill_dep, penguins$bill_len, use = "complete.obs") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.2350529 ``` ::: ::: . . . * Note: By default, `cor()` returns Pearson correlation . . . * Other correlations: * [Spearman's correlation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spearman's_rank_correlation_coefficient) * [Kendall rank correlation coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendall_rank_correlation_coefficient) * and more ## Making scatterplots ::: columns ::: {.column} * Use `geom_point()` * Displaying the joint (bivariate) distribution * What is the obvious flaw with this plot? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) theme_set(theme_light()) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_dep, y = bill_len)) + geom_point(color = "darkred") ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Making scatterplots: adjust the transparency ::: columns ::: {.column} * Adjust the transparency of points via `alpha` to visualize overlap * Provide better understanding of joint frequency * Especially important with larger datasets ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_dep, y = bill_len)) + geom_point(color = "darkred", alpha = 0.5) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Point color by a categorical variable ::: columns ::: {.column} * Map a categorical variable to `color` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_dep, y = bill_len, color = species)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Point color by a continuous variable ::: columns ::: {.column} * Map a continuous variable to `color` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_dep, y = bill_len, color = body_mass)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Color gradient for a continuous variable ::: columns ::: {.column} * Map a continuous variable to `color` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_dep, y = bill_len, color = body_mass)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + scale_color_gradient(low = "darkblue", high = "darkorange") ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Point size by a continuous variable ::: columns ::: {.column} * Map a continuous variable to `size` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_dep, y = bill_len, size = body_mass)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Point shape by a categorical variable ::: columns ::: {.column} * Map a categorical variable to `shape` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_dep, y = bill_len, shape = species)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Mapping multiple aesthetics to different variables ::: columns ::: {.column} * Each of `color`, `shape`, and `size`
is mapped to a different variable * 5 dimensions at once! * Be careful about this... ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_dep, y = bill_len, color = species, shape = island, size = body_mass)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Displaying trend line: linear regression ::: columns ::: {.column} * Display regression line for
`body_mass ~ flipper_len` * 95% confidence band by default * Estimating the conditional expectation of
`body_mass` | `flipper_len` * i.e., $\mathbb{E}[$ `body_mass` $\mid$ `flipper_len` $]$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass)) + geom_point(color = "darkred", alpha = 0.5) + geom_smooth(method = "lm") ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Visualizing joint density Data: shot attempts by the [Sabrina Ionescu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabrina_Ionescu) in the 2023 WNBA season * Each row is a shot attempt by Sabrina Ionescu in the 2023 WNBA season * Categorical variables: `scoring_play`, `shot_type` * Quantitative variables: `shot_x`, `shot_y`, `shot_distance`, `score_value` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ionescu_shots <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/qntkhvn/36-315-summer26/refs/heads/master/data/ionescu-shots.csv") |> filter(shot_y < 35) # remove some outliers glimpse(ionescu_shots) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 614 Columns: 6 $ shot_x -10, 11, 2, -13, -18, 19, -1, 0, -1, -12, -1, -14, -7, -… $ shot_y 24, 23, 2, 21, 19, 16, 3, 2, 4, 5, 2, 21, 26, 14, 7, 6, … $ shot_distance 26.000000, 25.495098, 2.828427, 24.698178, 26.172505, 24… $ shot_type "Pullup Jump Shot", "Running Jump Shot", "Cutting Layup … $ scoring_play FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FAL… $ score_value 0, 3, 0, 0, 3, 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0, 3, 0, 2, 0, 3, 3, 0, 0,… ``` ::: ::: ## A subtle point about histogram ::: columns ::: {.column .fragment} By default, the bins are centered at the integers
Intervals are left-closed, right-open: -0.5 to 0.5, etc. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ionescu_shots |> ggplot(aes(x = shot_distance)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column .fragment} Specify the center of one bin (e.g. 0.5)
and use `closed = "left"` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ionescu_shots |> ggplot(aes(x = shot_distance)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, center = 0.5, closed = "left") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Visualizing joint density ::: columns ::: {.column} * Visualize joint distribution with a scatterplot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ionescu_shots |> ggplot(aes(x = shot_x, y = shot_y)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.3) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Review: 1D kernel density estimation ::: columns ::: {.column} * The KDE estimator is $$\displaystyle \hat{f}(x) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{h} K_h(x - x_i)$$ * Smooth out each observation into a small distribution (small "bump") * Kernel functions are pdfs * Put a copy of the kernel at each observation, then add them up * This is a mixture * Basis distributions are the scaled copies of the kernel, centered at the $x_i$'s * Weight of each mixture component is $1/n$ ::: ::: {.column}

![](../images/kde-bumps.png){height=550}
::: ::: ## Going from 1D to 2D density estimation In 1D: estimate density $f(x)$, assuming that $f(x)$ is _smooth_: $$ \hat{f}(x) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{h} K_h(x - x_i) $$ . . . In 2D: estimate joint density $f(x_1, x_2)$ $$\hat{f}(x_1, x_2) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{h_1h_2} K\left(\frac{x_1 - x_{i1}}{h_1}\right) K\left(\frac{x_2 - x_{i2}}{h_2}\right)$$ . . . For 2D: there are 2 bandwidths * $h_1$: controls smoothness as $X_1$ changes, holding $X_2$ fixed * $h_2$: controls smoothness as $X_2$ changes, holding $X_1$ fixed Gaussian kernels are still a popular choice ## Display densities for 2D data: contour plots Best known in topography: outlines (contours) denote levels of elevation
![](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5cb6391f7980b3404bf57113/1573157765676-YX6XBYP01AORIHYCTUSR/3d+Topp+Greenbelly.co.png){height=700}
## Create contours of 2D kernel density estimate ::: columns ::: {.column} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ionescu_shots |> ggplot(aes(x = shot_x, y = shot_y)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.3) + geom_density2d() + coord_fixed() ``` ::: * Use [`geom_density2d()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_density_2d.html) to display contour lines * Extend KDE for joint density estimates in 2D * Inner lines denote "peaks" * `coord_fixed()` forced a fixed ratio ::: ::: {.column} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-29-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Create contours of 2D kernel density estimate ::: columns ::: {.column} * Modify the binwidth ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ionescu_shots |> ggplot(aes(x = shot_x, y = shot_y)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.3) + geom_density2d(binwidth = 0.0001) + coord_fixed() ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-31-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Contours are difficult... what about heatmaps? ::: columns ::: {.column width="45%"} * Use [`stat_density_2d()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_density_2d.html) and the [`after_stat()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/aes_eval.html) function to make 2D KDE **heatmaps** * May be easier to read than nested lines with color ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ionescu_shots |> ggplot(aes(x = shot_x, y = shot_y)) + stat_density2d(aes(fill = after_stat(level)), geom = "polygon") + scale_fill_gradient(low = "darkblue", high = "gold") + coord_fixed() ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-32-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Use tiles instead ::: columns ::: {.column width="45%"} * Divide the space into a grid and color the grid according to high/low values ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ionescu_shots |> ggplot(aes(x = shot_x, y = shot_y)) + stat_density2d(aes(fill = after_stat(density)), geom = "tile", contour = FALSE) + scale_fill_gradient(low = "darkblue", high = "gold") + coord_fixed() ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="55%} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-33-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Hexagonal binning ::: columns ::: {.column width="45%"} * Use [`geom_hex()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_hex.html) to make **hexagonal heatmaps** * Need to have the [`hexbin`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/hexbin/index.html) package installed * 2D version of histogram ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ionescu_shots |> ggplot(aes(x = shot_x, y = shot_y)) + geom_hex() + scale_fill_gradient(low = "darkblue", high = "gold") + coord_fixed() ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-34-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## What about shooting efficiency? ::: columns ::: {.column width="45%"} * Compute a function of another variable inside hexagons with [`stat_summary_hex()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/stat_summary_2d.html) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ionescu_shots |> ggplot(aes(x = shot_x, y = shot_y, z = scoring_play, group = -1)) + stat_summary_hex(binwidth = c(2, 2), fun = mean, color = "black") + scale_fill_gradient(low = "darkblue", high = "gold") + coord_fixed() ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-35-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Linear regression Assume a __linear relationship__ for $Y = f(X)$ $$Y_{i}=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1} X_{i}+\epsilon_{i}, \quad \text { for } i=1,2, \dots, n$$ * $Y_i$ is the $i$th value for the **response** variable * $X_i$ is the $i$th value for the **predictor** variable . . . * $\beta_0$ is an unknown, constant **intercept** * average value for $Y$ if $X = 0$ (be careful sometimes...) * $\beta_1$ is an unknown, constant **slope** * change in average value for $Y$ for each one-unit increase in $X$ . . . * $\epsilon_i$ is the __random__ noise * assume **independent, identically distributed** (iid) from a normal distribution * $\epsilon_i \overset{iid}{\sim}N(0, \sigma^2)$ with constant variance $\sigma^2$ ## Linear regression estimation * Estimate the **conditional expection** for $Y$ (i.e., average value for $Y$ given the value for $X$) $$\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i] = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_i$$ . . . * Estimate the **best fitted** line with **ordinary least squares (OLS)** by minimizing the **residual sum of squares (RSS)** $$\text{RSS} \left(\beta_{0}, \beta_{1}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[Y_{i}-\left(\beta_{0}+\beta_{1} X_{i}\right)\right]^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_{i}-\beta_{0}-\beta_{1} X_{i}\right)^{2}$$ . . . $$\widehat{\beta}_{1}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(X_{i}-\bar{X}\right)\left(Y_{i}-\bar{Y}\right)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(X_{i}-\bar{X}\right)^{2}} = \frac{\textsf{Cov}(X,Y)}{\textsf{Var}(X)} \quad \text{ and } \quad \widehat{\beta}_{0}=\bar{Y}-\widehat{\beta}_{1} \bar{X}$$ ## Visual explanation of linear regression in 2D * Goal: find a "best fit" line that minimizes the vertical distance between the line and the data points * The vertical distance is known as a residual (difference between the actual y-value of a data point and the predicted y-value on the regression line) ::: columns ::: {.column} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-36-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-37-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Linear regression in `R` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins_lm <- lm(body_mass ~ flipper_len, data = penguins) summary(penguins_lm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = body_mass ~ flipper_len, data = penguins) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -1058.80 -259.27 -26.88 247.33 1288.69 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) -5780.831 305.815 -18.90 <2e-16 *** flipper_len 49.686 1.518 32.72 <2e-16 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 394.3 on 340 degrees of freedom (2 observations deleted due to missingness) Multiple R-squared: 0.759, Adjusted R-squared: 0.7583 F-statistic: 1071 on 1 and 340 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: ## Assessing assumptions of linear regression Simple linear regression assumes $Y_i \overset{\textsf{iid}}{\sim} N(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i, \sigma^2)$ * If this is true, then $Y_i - \hat{Y}_i \overset{\textsf{iid}}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2)$ . . . Plot residuals against fitted values $\hat{Y}_i$ * Assess linearity: any divergence from mean 0 * Asess equal variance: if $\sigma^2$ is homogeneous across predictions/fits $\hat{Y}_i$ . . . More difficult to assess independence and fixed $X$ assumptions * Make these assumptions based on subject-matter knowledge ## Plot residuals against predicted values ::: columns ::: {.column} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble(fitted = fitted(penguins_lm), resid = residuals(penguins_lm)) |> ggplot(aes(x = fitted, y = resid)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") ``` ::: * Conditional on the predicted values, residuals should have a mean of zero * Residuals should not display any pattern * Two things to look for: * Any trend around horizontal reference line? * Equal vertical spread? ::: ::: {.column} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-40-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Linear regression with categorical variables * A categorical variable of $k$ levels is encoded into $k-1$ indicator/dummy variables . . . * Example: Penguins species (3 levels: Adelie, Chinstrap, Gentoo) * Indicators for Chinstrap and Gentoo: $I_C$ and $I_G$ * If $I_C = I_G = 0$, then the species must be Adelie (reference/baseline level) . . . * Model: $Y_i \overset{\textsf{iid}}{\sim} N(\beta_0 + \beta_C I_C + \beta_G I_G, \sigma^2)$ * $\beta_0$: mean for Adelie (reference level) * $\beta_0 + \beta_C$: mean for Chinstrap * $\beta_0 + \beta_G$: mean for Gentoo * Significant $\beta_C$: Chinstrap and Adelie are different * Significant $\beta_G$: Gentoo and Adelie are different * What about comparing Chinstrap and Gentoo? Need to fit a different model ## Linear regression with interactions * Setup: response $Y$ (`bill_dep`) and 2 predictors $X$ (`bill_len`, quantitative) and `species` (categorical) . . . * Model 1 (additive, no interaction): $Y_i \overset{\textsf{iid}}{\sim} N(\beta_0 + \beta_X X + \beta_C I_C + \beta_G I_G, \sigma^2)$
(Formula: `bill_dep ~ bill_len + species`) * The intercept for Adelie: $\beta_0$; for Chinstrap: $\beta_0 + \beta_C$; for Gentoo: $\beta_0 + \beta_G$ * The slope for all species: $\beta_X$ . . . * Model 2 (with interaction): $Y_i \overset{\textsf{iid}}{\sim} N(\beta_0 + \beta_X X + \beta_C I_C + \beta_G I_G + \beta_{CX} I_C X + \beta_{GX} I_G X, \sigma^2)$
(Formula: `bill_dep ~ bill_len + species + bill_len:species`) * The intercept for Adelie: $\beta_0$; for Chinstrap: $\beta_0 + \beta_C$; for Gentoo: $\beta_0 + \beta_G$ * The slope for Adelie: $\beta_X$; for Chinstrap: $\beta_X + \beta_{CX}$; for Gentoo: $\beta_X + \beta_{GX}$ * Significant coefficient for categorical variables by themselves $\rightarrow$ significantly different intercepts * Significant coefficient for interactions with categorical variables $\rightarrow$ significantly different slopes ## Visualizing additive model (no interaction) Model: `bill_dep ~ bill_len + species` Example of [Simpson’s paradox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simpson%27s_paradox): negative linear relationship between bill depth and bill length overall, but positive linear relationship within species ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} additive_lm <- lm(bill_dep ~ bill_len + species, data = penguins) intercepts <- c( coef(additive_lm)["(Intercept)"], coef(additive_lm)["(Intercept)"] + coef(additive_lm)["speciesChinstrap"], coef(additive_lm)["(Intercept)"] + coef(additive_lm)["speciesGentoo"] ) lines_tbl <- tibble(intercept = intercepts, slope = rep(coef(additive_lm)["bill_len"], 3), species = levels(penguins$species)) penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + geom_abline(data = lines_tbl, linewidth = 1.5, aes(intercept = intercept, slope = slope, color = species)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-41-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1152} ::: ::: ## Summarizing additive model ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(lm(bill_dep ~ bill_len + species, data = penguins)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = bill_dep ~ bill_len + species, data = penguins) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -2.4529 -0.6864 -0.0508 0.5519 3.5915 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 10.59218 0.68302 15.508 < 2e-16 *** bill_len 0.19989 0.01749 11.427 < 2e-16 *** speciesChinstrap -1.93319 0.22416 -8.624 2.55e-16 *** speciesGentoo -5.10602 0.19142 -26.674 < 2e-16 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 0.9533 on 338 degrees of freedom (2 observations deleted due to missingness) Multiple R-squared: 0.769, Adjusted R-squared: 0.7669 F-statistic: 375.1 on 3 and 338 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: ## Visualizing model with interaction Model: `bill_dep ~ bill_len + species + bill_len:species` Map `species` to the `color` aesthetic for `geom_smooth()` layer ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep, color = species)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-43-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1152} ::: ::: ## Summarizing model with interaction ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(lm(bill_dep ~ bill_len * species, data = penguins)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = bill_dep ~ bill_len * species, data = penguins) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -2.6574 -0.6675 -0.0524 0.5383 3.5032 Coefficients: Estimate Std. <script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
